sources.title: PDF The Frequency Distribution of Web Page Requests, Does it follow Zipf law?
sources.snippet: In Web applications, the distribution of web pages ranked by their popularity (frequency of requests in a large set of web pages) is believed to be a power law distribution known as Zipfs law.(G.K Zipf, Human Behavior and the Principle of Least Effort.

sources.title: Zipf's Law: Definition, Formula & Caching Applications
sources.snippet: Zipf's Law states that the frequency of an item is inversely proportional to its rank. Learn how this power-law distribution models content popularity in proactive caching.

sources.title: Zipf's Law and Cache Hit Ratios: Why Your Caching Math Fails When ...
sources.snippet: We assume that web traffic naturally obeys Zipf's Law. When real-world traffic breaks that assumption due to bot activity, cryptographic lookups, or flash crowds—standard cache sizing formulas completely fall apart. Let's look at why cache math relies on power-law distributions and what happens when reality refuses to cooperate.

sources.title: Using Causality for Enhanced Prediction of Web Traffic Time Series
sources.snippet: Predicting web service traffic has significant social value, as it can be applied to various practical scenarios, including but not limited to dynamic resource scaling, load balancing, system anomaly detection, service-level agreement compliance, and fraud detection. Web service traffic is characterized by frequent and drastic fluctuations over time and are influenced by heterogeneous web user behaviors, making accurate prediction a challenging task.
